introduction: The promenade along the western castle wall began as a defensive passage and became a public walk, taking its present name in the 20th century. The documented record is thin, and the sources read give few dates.
chapters: A defensive passage on the wall

Time Out Budapest describes the Tóth Árpád Promenade as a route with a history of several centuries that grew out of a former defensive passage along the castle wall, on the western side of the Castle District. The page gives no construction dates and does not say who built the passage or when it first became a place for walking. The English Wikipedia article on Buda Castle describes a reconstruction of the castle's fortifications from the 1950s to 1966, and its article on the Bastion Promenade says the promenade was heavily damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt between 1966 and 1970.
From Bástya sétány to a named promenade

A Hungarian city-culture article records that in 1936 gardens still occupied the ground behind the wall, and that they were removed to make way for the Bástya sétány, the Bastion Promenade. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was cut into several sections. The Tóth Árpád sétány is described as the other half of the former Bástya sétány, while the Babits Mihály sétány came from the same division. The promenade now bears the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, who lived from 1886 to 1928 and wrote for the journal Nyugat. The pages consulted do not explain why he was chosen.

introduction: The Garden of Philosophers on Gellért Hill is a bronze sculpture group created by Nándor Wagner and given to Budapest by his widow. It was unveiled in October 2001 and has been damaged by thieves since.
chapters: Wagner and the idea of a philosophical garden

Nándor Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and studied at the Budapest art academy. After the suppression of the 1956 revolution he was admitted to Sweden, where he worked in Lund, and later settled in Mashiko in Japan, where he met his wife, the art student Chiyo. According to Wikipedia he created the Garden of Philosophy there as a spiritual message for present and future generations and said it was not made to earn money. XpatLoop reports that he unveiled the first statue, Laozi, in 1977 and the others during the 1980s in Japan.
A gift to Budapest, unveiled in 2001

Wagner died in 1997. Wikipedia says three sets were cast, for Japan, Hungary and the United States, and that the Hungarian set was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. The Hungarian magazine HVG describes the Budapest group as a gift from the sculptor's widow, and XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site. The Budapest sources describe eight life-size bronze figures facing a shared centre.
Theft and damage in 2006 and 2007

HVG reported in April 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma, were stolen from the hill, with damage estimated at about thirty million forints, according to the director of the Budapest Gallery. The article says that the previous October someone had removed five large bronze arc pieces that stood around the statues and had cut notches in the figures with a saw so that they could be broken off, but that an eyewitness interrupted them. It also notes that plaster moulds for recasting the statues exist in Japan. The sources read do not say what happened afterwards.

introduction: Palatinus opened in 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach and grew into one of the largest open-air baths in Europe. A 1937 expansion, postwar changes and a 2017 reconstruction shaped what visitors see today.
chapters: Founding on Margaret Island, 1919 to 1921

We Love Budapest records that the bath opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, with water from the island's thermal wells, which 19th-century drilling by Vilmos Zsigmondy had made possible. Károly Arvé and Márton Nagy designed the first beach, which had no reception building yet. Hungarian Wikipedia says it closed after a year so that construction could begin and that the new bath opened permanently in August 1921, with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools. Before the Second World War its continuous water surface of about five thousand square metres made it the largest outdoor bath in Europe, according to We Love Budapest.
The modernist expansion of 1937

In 1937 the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed the central changing building, a modernist block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with the wave pool. The plan was debated in public, and the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma against critics who wanted the park setting left intact. Wave pools were then still new in Budapest: We Love Budapest notes that the first in the city was at Csillaghegy in 1927 and that Palatinus was the third. The war later destroyed sculpture and a wall painting at the entrance.
Postwar changes and the 2017 reconstruction

After the war the bath was restored. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a ten-thousand-square-metre sunbathing lawn added in 1958, a new restaurant in 1965, an additional area with playgrounds and a football pitch in 1975, and a five-lane slide in the 1980s. A mosaic by Endre Bálint was added at the wave pool in the 1960s. In 2002 the pools received modern filtration, and in 2016-17 the monument-protected reconstruction by Archikon winterised the main building and added a covered section with thermal and wellness facilities, so the bath could work throughout the year. The destroyed Ady-poem wall painting was restored at the same time.

introduction: The Veli Bej Bath is an Ottoman bath of the 1570s that survived the end of Ottoman rule, passed to a Hospitaller order and was restored in the early 2010s. It now sits inside a hospital complex.
chapters: An Ottoman bath of 1574 to 1575

Budapest by Locals states that the oldest part of the Császár spa, the Turkish bath, was built by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha in 1574-75, and that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The page notes that Buda had roughly seven to nine baths during the 150 years of Ottoman rule and that several of the smaller ones did not survive. Another article reports that a commemorative plaque from the building of the bath remains on a wall.
The Hospitallers and József Hild

In 1806 the bath became the property of the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order, which expanded the original Ottoman buildings. A reconstruction led by József Hild between 1841 and 1848 enlarged the complex considerably and renamed it Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő. A 2018 article dates the Hild reconstruction to 1842 and describes the result as classicist. That article adds that in the 1970s the neighbouring hospital was extended with a modern wing that now encloses the small bath, which makes it hard to see from outside.
Restoration in the early 2010s

The Hospitaller order decided to restore the complex fully and to rebuild the original Ottoman bath, working with archaeologists and art historians. Budapest by Locals says the renovation was finished in 2011, while an article published in 2018 says the bath reopened in 2012, so the sources differ by a year. Original clay pipes laid by the Ottomans were found during the work, and archaeologists had them preserved so that they can be seen between the pools and the saunas. A small display of finds, including floor coverings, dishes and grindstones, was also assembled.

introduction: Aquaworld is a recent attraction, not a historic one: it opened in December 2008 as a water park and hotel complex. The sources read describe its opening and construction, and say little about the years since.
chapters: Opening in December 2008

A report from the water-park supplier Polin says the complex opened in December 2008 as the Ramada Resort - Aquaworld Budapest and describes it as Central Europe's largest indoor water theme park. The hotel had 261 rooms, with a separate building holding 48 apartments, and the leisure area was covered by a glass dome 73 metres wide and 21 metres high. The same report says the water park had 21 pools with a combined surface of 3,300 square metres, a figure that later travel guides do not repeat.
The designers and builders

The project manager was the company Eleven Kft, which chose Polin Waterparks and Pool Systems to supply the water park, slides, amusement elements and water engineering. The park has eleven slides with a total length of almost one kilometre, and six giant slides start from a slide tower next to the dome that is reached by a glass lift or by stairs, and the highest ride begins from 17 metres up. A conveyor-type lift carries the tubes back to the start. A later travel guide describes the resort as one of Europe's largest indoor water theme parks and still lists eleven slides, but gives different pool counts of 17 and 15, so the sources about the layout are not fully consistent.

introduction: Lupa Beach is a very recent addition to the Budapest area: a former quarry lake that became a beach resort in 2016 and was reopened on a larger scale in 2017. It lies just outside the city limits at Budakalász.
chapters: A quarry lake north of the city

Just Budapest describes Lake Lupa as a former quarry transformed into a recreational site, in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. XpatLoop, reporting in July 2016, called it a former quarry on the city's northern outskirts and said that swimming in the lake had previously been banned. The sources read do not say when the quarry was worked or when it closed.
The 2016 trial summer and the 2017 expansion

The developer was Károly Gerendai, who founded the Sziget Festival. XpatLoop reported that the resort was due to open officially on 14 July 2016 and that Gerendai described the first summer as a test period to gain experience for the following year. He had signed a 20-year lease with an option to buy, and catering and other services were contracted out, as at Sziget. We Love Budapest reported in May 2017 that the beach was reopening after the trial run with the swimmable shoreline quadrupled, so that the beach was about 2.5 kilometres long. Just Budapest also credits Gerendai with the 2017 development of the area.

introduction: The Római open-air bath stands in Óbuda on ground that belonged to the Roman town of Aquincum. The documented history the sources give is of a bath renewed in 1964 and modernised in 2000, with older claims best read as tradition.
chapters: Springs, mills and an old claim

The BKK listing for the bath says that the Romans already regarded the local springs as sacred and that chronicles from the time of King Matthias mention a hospital here. The listing does not cite a source for either statement, so they are best read as local tradition. Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part is more specific about the early 19th century: the neighbourhood of Rómaifürdő lies beside springs where mills once operated, and the riverside was then a popular centre of river life with water clean enough for swimming.
The renewed bath of 1964

Programturizmus states that the renovated Római Strandfürdő opened in 1964 and that it has kept the layout it had then. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that free public beaches on the Danube bank here, named Hungária, Duna and Tungsram, operated in the early 20th century, and that the official bathing places on the river were closed in 1973 because water quality had declined. The Római-part Danube beach, where swimming is not permitted, was opened by the district in 2021.
Modernisation around 2000

Programturizmus records that in 2000 the three pools of the bath were modernised and fitted with filtered circulation. The main pool became an adventure pool with a slide, neck showers and bubble jets, and the children's pool became a playground. The bath is an open-air, seasonal summer facility, and a 2025 news report named it among the bathing places that closed at the end of the season on 31 August.
